title: Yours, yours, yours
told: a sakhi of Guru Nanak, a traditional story

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? what do you find yourself thinking about while you work?
options: ha. then this one is for you. listen.
then listen. this one is about what’s underneath.

steps.line: As a young man in Sultanpur, Guru Nanak worked as a storekeeper, weighing out grain from the governor’s store.
steps.label: a traditional story

steps.line: One day he was measuring grain for a customer, counting each measure aloud: one, two, three…

steps.q: He’s counting the measures aloud: eleven, twelve… What do you think stops his counting?
o: A beggar who comes to the door
The call to prayer from the mosque
steps.why: Thirteen is tera in Punjabi, and tera also means yours. Nanak had the storekeeper’s job through his sister Nanaki’s husband, Jai Ram, who worked for the governor, Daulat Khan Lodi.

steps.line: At thirteen he said tera, and stopped counting. Tera, tera, he kept saying, yours, yours, and kept pouring out the grain.

steps.q: Why would the word tera, “yours,” carry him away?
o: He’d simply lost track of the count
He felt sorry for a poor customer
It reminded him all is God’s
steps.why: Yours, God’s. The grain, the scale, the hands that held it.

steps.line: Someone ran to the governor: Nanak is giving away the store! The governor ordered the accounts checked.

steps.q: The clerks count every sack. What do you think they find?
steps.why: Not a grain was missing. Giving with a remembering heart didn’t empty the store.

steps.line: The clerks counted everything. Nothing was missing. In many tellings, there was even more than before.
Sikhs build a life on three pillars: naam japna, remembering God all day long. Kirat karni, honest work. And vand chakna, sharing.
steps.label: today

steps.line: One common way is simran, remembering on the breath: wahe on the in-breath, guru on the out-breath, while you cook, drive or work.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Not long after, Nanak went into the river Bein and vanished for three days. What did he say when he came back?
steps.why: Sikhs remember those days as his call. He came back saying there is no Hindu and no Muslim, only people of the One, and soon left the store to travel and teach.

steps.q: Wahe on the in-breath, guru on the out-breath. Together it’s Waheguru, a Sikh name for God. What does it mean?
steps.why: Wah is a cry of wonder, like “wow.” Guru is often explained as the one who leads from darkness to light. A name for God that starts in amazement.

say: here’s what i love. guru nanak didn’t leave the shop to remember god. he remembered right there on the scale, in the middle of work.
that’s naam japna, the third pillar, and many sikhs name it first. without it, work can turn to pride and giving to show. with it, everything becomes tera: yours.

steps.q: From the story, why does remembering “tera, yours” keep giving humble?
o: The grain belonged to the governor
What you give was never yours
steps.why: Tera turns “look what i gave” into “it was yours all along.”

today.say: today, tie remembering to something you do anyway: the kettle, the commute, the dishes. it’s your choice how: just watch your breath, or, if you like, wahe in, guru out.
options: then let the kettle remind you. tera, yours.
that’s okay. just breathe, and remember what’s real for you.

tomorrow.line: two weeks done. next, the people you sit with.

card.keepWhy: Tera, tera. All of it, yours.
sources: Janamsakhi tradition of Guru Nanak as storekeeper (modi) at the modikhana of Nawab Daulat Khan Lodi in Sultanpur, and the “tera” sakhi
Sikh teaching of the three pillars: naam japna, kirat karni, vand chhakna
Naam simran with Waheguru on the breath
check: The tera story and the audit finding nothing missing (in some tellings a surplus) are tradition; labeled.
Wahe on the in-breath, guru on the out-breath is one common simran method, not the only one.
